A legacy config: routing object becomes a composite aiTargets entry. Each entry of its targets[] list becomes a standalone aiTargets entry of its own, and the composite references them by id. Before: targets: - id: custom_config config: strategy: mode: loadbalance targets: - provider: openai api_key: ${OPENAI_API_KEY} override_params: model: gpt-6-luna - provider: openrouter api_key: ${OPENROUTER_API_KEY} override_params: model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5 After: aiTargets: - id: custom_config-a provider: openai apiKey: ${OPENAI_API_KEY} options: model: gpt-6-luna - id: custom_config-b provider: openrouter apiKey: ${OPENROUTER_API_KEY} options: model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5 - id: custom_config strategy: loadbalance routes: - target: custom_config-a - target: custom_config-b No inline per-route overrides Composite routes cannot carry override_params — they reference a concrete target by id. Set options on the route targets instead, as above. Weights are expressed with routes[].weight (loadbalance only). See Routing, Retries & Timeouts for fallback vs loadbalance semantics and validation rules.

Legacy config.beforeRequestHooks become entries in the top-level guardrails: list, attached to a target by name. Before: targets: - id: custom_config_guardrails config: provider: openai api_key: ${OPENAI_API_KEY} override_params: model: gpt-6-luna beforeRequestHooks: - type: guardrail id: mistral_check deny: true checks: - id: mistral.moderateContent parameters: credentials: apiKey: ${MISTRAL_API_KEY} categories: - pii - sexual - hate_and_discrimination After: aiTargets: - id: custom_config_guardrails provider: openai apiKey: ${OPENAI_API_KEY} options: model: gpt-6-luna guardrails: [custom_config_guardrails-moderation] # Dedicated moderation-only target. runModeration() falls back to OpenAI's # default baseURL when settings.baseURL is unset, so it must be explicit here. - id: mistral-moderation provider: mistral apiKey: ${MISTRAL_API_KEY} settings: baseURL: https://api.mistral.ai/v1 guardrails: - name: custom_config_guardrails-moderation type: llm mode: moderation-api target: mistral-moderation model: mistral-moderation-latest categories: [pii, sexual, hate_and_discrimination] threshold: 0.8 onFail: deny onError: allow Fail-open choice onError: allow means a moderation-endpoint outage silently disables enforcement on that target. Use onError: deny when the check must be fail-closed. Full reference, including pre/post/both phases, redact and log actions, and streaming behaviour: Guardrails.

Retries are on by default. Chat completions and the Responses API use 3 total attempts with backoff. Set retry: { maxAttempts: 1 } on a target to keep the legacy single-shot behaviour. Unknown request parameters are dropped and logged, instead of being forwarded to the provider. Error bodies have a fixed shape. Upstream failures return the 502 JSON documented in AI-Link errors — not the legacy gateway's error envelope. Streaming failures before the first byte return 502. The legacy path could deliver a partially-committed stream; the new path detects a pre-header failure and can retry or fall back. debug and logUpstream apply to aiTargets only. Legacy targets ignore them. hub.ailink_* settings do not affect aiTargets. They only configure the legacy AI gateway subprocess. Images and audio make a single attempt. Retries and composite fallback cover chat completions and the Responses API only.

Legacy target ids inventoried (deprecation warnings, Admin Panel AI-Link tab) No id to be migrated is used on /v1/embeddings, /v1/completions or /v1/rerank aiTargets entry created for each legacy target, with the same id Provider names canonicalized (perplexity-ai → perplexity, mistral-ai → mistral, together-ai → togetherai, fireworks-ai → fireworks, x-ai → xai) Provider-specific fields moved under settings: options.model set on every concrete target Custom endpoints converted to provider: openai-compatible + settings.baseURL (with /v1) Legacy config: routing objects converted to composite entries Legacy beforeRequestHooks converted to guardrails: entries and attached retry / requestTimeout reviewed (timeouts shared across a route's retries) Hub restarted; startup schema validation passes Each target tested with curl, including stream: true No deprecated legacy target warnings remain for migrated ids Legacy entries deleted; /ready shows the ai_gateway check skipped: true Unused hub.ailink_* environment overrides removed
How the Hub decides which upstream call to make, when it tries again, and how long it waits.

A composite aiTargets entry fans a single x-target id out to several concrete targets: aiTargets: - id: prod-chat strategy: fallback # or: loadbalance routes: - target: openai - target: anthropic weight: 1 # weights apply to loadbalance only Field Required Description id yes Value of the x-target header; takes priority over a legacy target of the same id strategy yes fallback or loadbalance routes yes Non-empty list of { target: <concrete aiTarget id>, weight?: number } requestTimeout no Inherited by any route that has no requestTimeout of its own debug no Applied to every route it executes, unless the route overrides the flag Validation rules, enforced at startup: retry: next to strategy:/routes: is rejected — attach it to the routes (aiTargets composite '<id>' cannot declare retry — attach it to its routes instead). guardrails: next to strategy:/routes: is rejected — attach them to the routes (aiTargets composite '<id>' cannot declare guardrails — attach them to its routes). Routes must reference an existing concrete target. Unknown ids and nested composites are rejected. id must be unique across aiTargets.
Routes are attempted in configuration order: aiTargets: - id: prod-chat strategy: fallback routes: - target: openai - target: azure-openai-chat - target: anthropic

The first route is picked weighted-randomly; the remaining routes follow in descending weight order (equal weights keep configuration order) so a failed pick still has an ordered fallback chain: aiTargets: - id: prod-chat strategy: loadbalance routes: - target: openai weight: 3 - target: anthropic weight: 1 weight must be greater than 0 and defaults to 1.

After a route exhausts its own retries, the Hub moves to the next route only if: the failure is retryable — HTTP 429, HTTP 5xx, a timeout, or a network error (ECONNREFUSED, ECONNRESET, ETIMEDOUT, ECONNABORTED, ENOTFOUND, EAI_AGAIN), and nothing has been streamed to the client yet, and there is another route left. Non-retryable failures — 400, 401, 403, 422, and any other 4xx — stop the chain immediately, even if later routes are configured: a bad API key or a missing model will not be fixed by another provider. A client disconnect is never retried and never falls back. Composite routing applies to chat completions and the Responses API. Image generation, audio speech, audio transcription and audio translation make a single attempt against the requested target and ignore composites.
documents.s: When a request moves to the next route

documents.t: Retries are owned by the AI engine itself — there is no hidden provider-level retry underneath — so they compose predictably with composite fallback and telemetry. Global defaults (hub.http_client.retry): hub: http_client: retry: maxAttempts: 3 # 1 initial attempt + 2 retries initialDelayMs: 500 maxDelayMs: 5000 backoffMultiplier: 2 Per-target override — fields you omit inherit the global value: aiTargets: - id: flaky-provider provider: openai apiKey: ${OPENAI_API_KEY} retry: maxAttempts: 5 initialDelayMs: 1000 options: model: gpt-6-luna - id: single-shot provider: anthropic apiKey: ${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY} retry: maxAttempts: 1 # disables retries for this target options: model: claude-sonnet-5-5 Backoff is equal-jitter exponential: delay n is 50–100 % of min(maxDelayMs, initialDelayMs × backoffMultiplier^n). The jitter avoids a thundering herd against a shared upstream outage. Retry scope: chat completions and the Responses API, including their streaming paths.

Timeout precedence for a single route: the route's own requestTimeout the composite's requestTimeout (when the requested id is a composite) hub.http_client.timeout (default 120000) requestTimeout: 0 disables the timeout entirely for that target. Two behaviours to plan for: All retries of one route share that route's timeout budget. The timer is armed once per route, not per attempt — retrying does not grant fresh headroom. A composite's requestTimeout is inherited per route; it does not span the whole chain. A live stream's timeout covers time-to-first-byte only, not the whole stream — unless a blocking post-phase guardrail forces internal buffering, in which case it covers the entire generation (see Guardrails). Raising attempts and timeouts together If you raise maxAttempts (or the backoff delays) on a target whose upstream is slow, raise requestTimeout as well. With a shared budget, a request that would have finished inside 120 s across 3 attempts can now exceed it.

prod-chat is a fallback composite over routes A (openai) and B (anthropic), with the default retry policy (maxAttempts: 3): Route A, attempt 1 → upstream answers 429. Retryable, attempts remain → backoff, retry. Route A, attempt 2 → upstream answers 503. Retryable → backoff, retry. Route A, attempt 3 → upstream answers 503. Retryable, but this route's attempts are exhausted → the Hub logs that route A failed retryably and moves to route B. Route B, attempt 1 → 200. The client receives route B's response. Nothing has been streamed to the client at any point, which is what makes steps 1–3 invisible to it. If route B had also failed retryably, the client would get a 502 describing the last failure.
documents.s: What a fallback chain looks like

documents.t: Each composite attempt is recorded individually in the runtime usage tracker: one error record per failed attempt, and recordSuccess (or a terminal recordError) on the last executed target. Consequently a composite that retries N times inflates the AI-Link request/error totals by N−1 compared with what a single logical request would otherwise count. That inflation is also tracked explicitly as fallback attempts, shown in the Admin Panel AI-Link tab, next to the per-target tables of requests, errors and latency. Deprecation warnings are separate: they appear as aiLink log lines whenever a request is served by a legacy target.
ProActions Hub provides comprehensive logging capabilities powered by Winston. This guide covers configuration, log types, and best practices for monitoring and compliance.
logging: format: json defaultLogLevel: info types: access: enabled: true console: true error: enabled: true console: true This enables basic access and error logging to console in JSON format.

logging: format: string # Log format: 'json' or 'text' text_format: string # Custom text format template defaultLogLevel: string # Default log level logDirectory: string # Directory for log files filePrefix: string # Prefix for log filenames fileRotation: boolean # Enable file rotation maxFileSize: string # Max size per log file maxFiles: string # Retention period sensitiveData: array # Keywords to filter logTrace: boolean # Include stack traces types: object # Per-type configurations

logging: format: json Example output: { "timestamp": "2024-01-15T10:30:00.123Z", "level": "info", "message": "AI request completed", "module": "aiLink", "target": "openai", "model": "gpt-6-luna", "promptTokens": 15, "completionTokens": 25, "totalTokens": 40 } Advantages: Easy to parse and query Works well with log aggregation tools Structured data for analytics Better for production environments

logging: format: text text_format: "${timestamp} [${level}] [${module}]: ${message}" Example output: 2024-01-15T10:30:00.123Z [info] [aiLink]: AI request completed Advantages: Human-readable Good for development Easier to read in terminal

Supported log levels (highest to lowest priority): Level Description Use Case error Critical errors requiring attention Production issues, exceptions warn Warning conditions Deprecated features, recoverable errors info Informational messages Request tracking, business events debug Detailed debugging information Development, troubleshooting verbose Very detailed information Deep debugging silly Most granular logs Rarely used
logging: defaultLogLevel: info This sets the level for log types that don't specify their own level. Production Recommendation Use info or warn in production. Use debug only for troubleshooting.
ProActions Hub supports six log types, each configurable independently:

HTTP request/response logs. logging: types: access: enabled: true console: true file: true level: info Logged information: HTTP method and URL Status code Response time Client IP address User agent Request ID Username (if authenticated) Example: { "timestamp": "2024-01-15T10:30:00.123Z", "level": "info", "message": "POST /v1/chat/completions 200 1234ms", "method": "POST", "url": "/v1/chat/completions", "statusCode": 200, "responseTime": 1234, "ip": "192.168.1.100", "userAgent": "ProActions-Client/1.0", "requestId": "abc123", "username": "john.doe" }

Application errors and exceptions. logging: types: error: enabled: true console: true file: true level: error Logged information: Error message Stack trace (if logTrace: true) Request context Error code Module where error occurred Example: { "timestamp": "2024-01-15T10:30:00.123Z", "level": "error", "message": "Failed to connect to AI provider", "error": "ECONNREFUSED", "stack": "Error: ECONNREFUSED...", "module": "aiLink", "target": "openai" }

AI operations and token usage tracking. logging: types: aiLink: enabled: true console: true file: false level: info logPrompt: false # Include prompts and effective request params in logs logResponse: false # Include responses in logs logUpstream: false # Include provider-native HTTP request/response bodies Logged information: Target and provider Model used Token usage (prompt, completion, total) Request duration Optional: prompt, response, and upstream wire bodies For aiTargets, three flags control the debug payloads attached to a request record (success or terminal error): Flag Adds to the record Contents logPrompt ai.prompt, ai.requestParams The messages/input actually sent (after pre-phase guardrail redaction), and the effective request config — options merged with the body, minus content keys, plus providerOptions logResponse ai.response The assembled text for a stream, or the response messages/output otherwise logUpstream ai.upstream.request, ai.upstream.response The provider-native wire bodies as posted by the SDK; on failure also the upstream error's url, statusCode, requestBodyValues and responseBody { "timestamp": "2024-01-15T10:30:00.123Z", "level": "info", "message": "AI request completed", "module": "aiLink", "target": "openai", "provider": "openai", "model": "gpt-6-luna", "promptTokens": 150, "completionTokens": 250, "totalTokens": 400, "duration": 1234 } Binary payloads (data URLs, long bare base64, Buffer/Uint8Array) are elided to a short placeholder; text is never truncated. Per-target overrides​ All three flags can be overridden per aiTargets entry, including on a composite (whose values apply to its routes): aiTargets: - id: openai provider: openai apiKey: ${OPENAI_API_KEY} debug: logUpstream: true # this target only options: model: gpt-6-luna Precedence: route → composite → global. An explicit false on a target beats a broader true. Prompt/Response/Upstream Logging Only enable logPrompt, logResponse and logUpstream for debugging. These logs can contain sensitive data — including full provider request/response bodies — and consume significant storage. Legacy targets debug and logUpstream apply to aiTargets only; legacy targets: entries ignore them. Every request served by a legacy target logs one warn-level aiLink line — AI-Link request served via deprecated legacy target — migrate '<id>' to aiTargets — so migration progress is visible without extra instrumentation.

HTTP proxy operations. logging: types: proxy: enabled: true console: true file: false level: info Logged information: Proxy target ID and URL Request path Response status Request duration Example: { "timestamp": "2024-01-15T10:30:00.123Z", "level": "info", "message": "Proxy request completed", "module": "proxy", "target": "deepl", "targetUrl": "https://api.deepl.com/v2/translate", "path": "/", "statusCode": 200, "duration": 456 }

YouTube API operations. logging: types: youtube: enabled: true console: true file: false level: info Logged information: Account ID Operation type (auth, upload, etc.) Success/failure status Video ID (for uploads) Example: { "timestamp": "2024-01-15T10:30:00.123Z", "level": "info", "message": "Video uploaded successfully", "module": "youtube", "account": "main", "videoId": "dQw4w9WgXcQ", "title": "My Video" }

Tool operations (content extraction, etc.). logging: types: tools: enabled: true console: true file: false level: info Logged information: Tool ID and type Operation parameters Success/failure status Processing time Example: { "timestamp": "2024-01-15T10:30:00.123Z", "level": "info", "message": "Content extraction completed", "module": "tools", "tool": "extract", "url": "https://example.com/article", "duration": 789 }
logging: logDirectory: logs filePrefix: app fileRotation: true maxFileSize: 10m maxFiles: 14d
When file logging is enabled for a log type, files are created with this pattern: logs/ ├── app-access-2024-01-15.log ├── app-error-2024-01-15.log ├── app-aiLink-2024-01-15.log └── ...

With rotation enabled: Files rotate daily Files rotate when they reach maxFileSize Old files are deleted after maxFiles period Files are compressed after rotation (gzip) Example maxFileSize values: 10m - 10 megabytes 100m - 100 megabytes 1g - 1 gigabyte Example maxFiles values: 7d - 7 days 14d - 14 days 30d - 30 days 10 - Keep 10 files
ProActions Hub automatically filters sensitive information from logs.
logging: sensitiveData: - password - token - apiKey - authorization - key - secret
Sensitive values are replaced with [FILTERED]: Before filtering: { "apiKey": "sk-abc123xyz", "password": "myPassword123" } After filtering: { "apiKey": "[FILTERED]", "password": "[FILTERED]" }
Add custom patterns: logging: sensitiveData: - password - token - apiKey - ssn - creditCard - privateKey

logging: logTrace: false When true, error logs include full stack traces. Production Warning Stack traces may expose sensitive information about your application's internal structure. Only enable for debugging.

logging: format: json defaultLogLevel: info logDirectory: logs filePrefix: proactions fileRotation: true maxFileSize: 100m maxFiles: 30d logTrace: false sensitiveData: - password - token - apiKey - authorization - key - secret types: access: enabled: true console: false file: true level: info error: enabled: true console: true file: true level: error aiLink: enabled: true console: false file: true level: info logPrompt: false logResponse: false proxy: enabled: true console: false file: true level: info youtube: enabled: true console: false file: true level: info tools: enabled: true console: false file: true level: info

logging: format: text text_format: "${timestamp} [${level}] [${module}]: ${message}" defaultLogLevel: debug logTrace: true types: access: enabled: true console: true file: false level: debug error: enabled: true console: true file: false level: error aiLink: enabled: true console: true file: false level: debug logPrompt: true logResponse: true proxy: enabled: true console: true file: false level: debug youtube: enabled: true console: true file: false level: debug tools: enabled: true console: true file: false level: debug
Podman: podman logs -f proactionshub Docker: docker compose logs -f
# View all logs tail -f logs/app-access-*.log # View specific log type tail -f logs/app-error-*.log # View logs with jq (for JSON) tail -f logs/app-aiLink-*.log | jq '.'
Using jq (JSON format): tail -f logs/app-access-*.log | jq 'select(.level == "error")' Using grep (text format): tail -f logs/app-access-*.log | grep ERROR

For JSON logs, configure Filebeat to ship logs to Elasticsearch: # filebeat.yml filebeat.inputs: - type: log enabled: true paths: - /path/to/logs/app-*.log json.keys_under_root: true json.add_error_key: true output.elasticsearch: hosts: ["elasticsearch:9200"]

The Proxy module enables HTTP request forwarding to configured target services. This is useful for routing requests through ProActions Hub to external APIs while maintaining centralized authentication and logging.

A basic proxy requires an ID and target URL: proxies: - id: deepl url: https://api.deepl.com/v2/translate options: secure: true changeOrigin: true headers: Authorization: ${DEEPL_AUTHORIZATION} Set the environment variable: DEEPL_AUTHORIZATION="DeepL-Auth-Key your-api-key"

Forward requests using the proxy endpoint: curl -X POST http://localhost:${PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT}/proxy/forward/deepl \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "text": ["Hello, world!"], "target_lang": "ES" }' The request path after /proxy/forward/{id} is appended to the target URL.

Each proxy in the proxies array has this structure: proxies: - id: string # Required: Unique identifier url: string # Required: Target URL remove_source_headers: array # Optional: Headers to strip options: object # Optional: http-proxy options
Field Description id Unique identifier used in the proxy path (/proxy/forward/{id}) url Target URL to forward requests to
Field Description Default remove_source_headers Array of header names to remove from forwarded requests [] options Configuration options passed to http-proxy {}
The options field accepts all http-proxy configuration options. Common options:
options: secure: true # Verify SSL certificates changeOrigin: true # Change origin header to target URL
Add headers to forwarded requests: options: headers: Authorization: ${API_KEY} X-Custom-Header: value User-Agent: ProActions-Hub/1.0
options: timeout: 30000 # Socket timeout (ms) proxyTimeout: 30000 # Proxy timeout (ms)
options: ws: true # Enable WebSocket proxying

proxies: - id: deepl url: https://api.deepl.com/v2/translate options: secure: true changeOrigin: true headers: Authorization: ${DEEPL_AUTHORIZATION} Usage: curl -X POST http://localhost:${PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT}/proxy/forward/deepl \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "text": ["Hello, world!"], "target_lang": "ES" }'

proxies: - id: azure-openai url: https://your-resource.openai.azure.com options: secure: true changeOrigin: true headers: api-key: ${AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY} Usage: curl -X POST http://localhost:${PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT}/proxy/forward/azure-openai/openai/deployments/gpt-6.1-sol/chat/completions?api-version=2024-02-15-preview \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}] }' AI-Link vs Proxy For AI services, prefer using AI-Link configuration which provides normalization and additional features. Use proxy for non-AI APIs or when you need direct passthrough.

proxies: - id: openai url: https://api.openai.com/v1 options: secure: true changeOrigin: true headers: Authorization: ${OPENAI_AUTHORIZATION} Environment variable: OPENAI_AUTHORIZATION="Bearer sk-your-api-key" Usage: curl -X POST http://localhost:${PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT}/proxy/forward/openai/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "gpt-6-luna", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}] }'
proxies: - id: external-api url: https://api.example.com options: secure: true changeOrigin: true headers: X-API-Key: ${EXTERNAL_API_KEY} Accept: application/json

Strip headers from the original request before forwarding: proxies: - id: secure-proxy url: https://api.example.com remove_source_headers: - x-forwarded-for - x-real-ip - authorization options: headers: Authorization: ${TARGET_API_KEY} This prevents client headers from being forwarded to the target.

Configure SSL certificate validation: proxies: - id: custom-tls url: https://api.example.com options: secure: true ssl: rejectUnauthorized: true ca: ${CA_CERT_PATH} cert: ${CLIENT_CERT_PATH} key: ${CLIENT_KEY_PATH}
proxies: - id: with-redirects url: https://api.example.com options: followRedirects: true maxRedirects: 5

For dynamic target resolution based on request: proxies: - id: dynamic-target url: https://api.example.com options: router: true # Custom routing logic Advanced Routing For complex routing logic, you may need to extend the proxy controller. Contact your development team for custom implementations.

The proxy appends the request path after the target URL: Configuration: proxies: - id: api url: https://api.example.com/v2 Request: GET /proxy/forward/api/users/123 Forwarded to: GET https://api.example.com/v2/users/123

To forward to the root of the target: Configuration: proxies: - id: api url: https://api.example.com Request: GET /proxy/forward/api/v2/users/123 Forwarded to: GET https://api.example.com/v2/users/123
Always use environment variables for API keys: proxies: - id: secure url: https://api.example.com options: headers: Authorization: ${API_KEY} # Good # Authorization: sk-abc123 # Bad - never hardcode
Always enable SSL verification for production: options: secure: true # Good - verify SSL certificates # secure: false # Bad - only for development

Remove sensitive headers before forwarding: proxies: - id: filtered url: https://api.example.com remove_source_headers: - authorization - cookie - x-api-key options: headers: Authorization: ${TARGET_API_KEY}
Use changeOrigin to prevent CORS issues: options: changeOrigin: true # Sets Host header to target URL

Proxy operations are logged when proxy logging is enabled: logging: types: proxy: enabled: true console: true file: false level: info Log output includes: Proxy target ID and URL Request method and path Response status code Request duration Error details (if applicable) See Logging Configuration for details.

# Test GET request curl http://localhost:${PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT}/proxy/forward/deepl # Test POST request curl -X POST http://localhost:${PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT}/proxy/forward/deepl \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"text": ["Hello"], "target_lang": "ES"}'
If Swagger is enabled: Navigate to http://localhost:${PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT}/docs Find the /proxy/forward/{target}/* endpoint Enter target ID and path Execute test request
Enable proxy logging and check logs: # Podman podman logs -f proactionshub | grep proxy # Docker docker compose logs -f | grep proxy
Error: Proxy target not found: xyz Solution: Verify the proxy ID in config.yaml matches the URL path.

Error: unable to verify the first certificate Solution: Set secure: false for testing (not recommended for production) Configure proper CA certificates Verify the target URL uses valid SSL certificates
Error: socket hang up or timeout errors Solution: Increase timeout settings: options: timeout: 60000 proxyTimeout: 60000
Error: Cross-origin request blocked Solution: Ensure changeOrigin: true is set: options: changeOrigin: true
Issue: Custom headers not appearing at target Solution: Check remove_source_headers is not removing them Add headers explicitly in options.headers Verify header names are correct (case-sensitive)

Issue: Incorrect path at target Solution: Review proxy URL configuration: Ensure target URL doesn't have trailing slash if not needed Verify request path structure Check that path components are correctly joined
Use environment variables for all credentials Enable SSL verification in production Set appropriate timeouts to prevent hanging requests Use descriptive IDs for easy identification
Remove sensitive headers before forwarding Add authentication headers in proxy configuration Use changeOrigin to prevent header leakage Enable logging for audit trails
Set reasonable timeouts based on target API Configure connection pooling if supported Monitor proxy logs for performance issues Use keepAlive for better performance
Configure error handling appropriately Set retry logic if needed (custom implementation) Monitor target availability through health checks Log all proxy operations for troubleshooting

ProActions HUB_VOICE_AGENT steps open a live audio session instead of a request/response completion. The browser cannot reach OpenAI directly in a centralized-key deployment, and a proxy cannot relay WebRTC media, so the Hub provides an authenticated WebSocket relay to the OpenAI Realtime API.

The Hub owns exactly two upgrade paths: /realtime — the canonical path, used when the reverse proxy strips every external prefix. /proactions/realtime — for deployments whose ingress strips only the app prefix and leaves the ProActions prefix in place. No deeper prefix is accepted. A request to e.g. /swing/proactions/realtime must be rewritten by the ingress before it reaches the Hub. Realtime is disabled by default, both globally and on every target. Enabling it requires all three of: auth.enabled: true with auth.type: token or auth.type: edapi an explicit origin policy a safety-identifier secret of at least 32 bytes See Voice Agents for the client side of HUB_VOICE_AGENT.

Main authentication enabled with auth.type: token or auth.type: edapi. Realtime authentication is stateless — it uses no HTTP sessions, no cookies, and no admin-key fallback. A Bearer <non-empty token> is required in both HTTP and WebSocket credentials, and malformed authorization prefixes are rejected outright. An exact origin policy. allowedOrigins lists the exact origins permitted to open a relay session. CORS configuration does not grant Realtime access. A 32-byte secret. safetyIdentifierSecret must be at least 32 UTF-8 bytes. The Hub derives the provider-side safety identifier from the authenticated principal; it never sends a principal, CMS token, article or action identifier to OpenAI. hub: realtime: enabled: true allowedOrigins: - https://swing.your-env.em-cms.cloud allowMissingOrigin: false safetyIdentifierSecret: ${REALTIME_SAFETY_IDENTIFIER_SECRET} allowMissingOrigin: true is only for controlled non-browser clients or tests: it permits an absent Origin header but never accepts an invalid present one.

The checked-in disabled defaults are the operational reference: hub: realtime: enabled: false allowedOrigins: [] allowMissingOrigin: false safetyIdentifierSecret: ${REALTIME_SAFETY_IDENTIFIER_SECRET} admissionTimeoutMs: 9000 providerConnectTimeoutMs: 8000 maxActiveSessions: 100 maxActiveSessionsPerPrincipal: 2 maxSessionDurationMs: 600000 maxAllowedSessionDurationMs: 3600000 idleTimeoutMs: 120000 maxMessageBytes: 1048576 maxBytesPerSecond: 2097152 trafficBurstBytes: 4194304 pauseBufferedBytes: 524288 resumeBufferedBytes: 131072 maxBufferedBytes: 1048576 backpressureTimeoutMs: 10000 heartbeatIntervalMs: 30000 heartbeatTimeoutMs: 10000 shutdownGraceMs: 5000 Setting Default Purpose admissionTimeoutMs 9000 Total admission budget, including authentication and provider readiness. providerConnectTimeoutMs 8000 Provider-side connection and readiness budget inside admission. maxActiveSessions 100 Global pending plus active admission limit. maxActiveSessionsPerPrincipal 2 Per-principal pending plus active relay session limit. maxSessionDurationMs 600000 Default maximum relay session duration. maxAllowedSessionDurationMs 3600000 Global cap for any effective session duration. idleTimeoutMs 120000 Maximum application-idle period; control ping/pong does not reset it. maxMessageBytes 1048576 Maximum complete text or binary message size. maxBytesPerSecond 2097152 Sustained per-direction byte rate. trafficBurstBytes 4194304 Per-direction token-bucket burst allowance. pauseBufferedBytes 524288 Destination queue high-water threshold that pauses the source. resumeBufferedBytes 131072 Destination queue low-water threshold that resumes the source. maxBufferedBytes 1048576 Destination queue hard limit. backpressureTimeoutMs 10000 Maximum continuous high-water duration. heartbeatIntervalMs 30000 Client- and provider-side ping interval. heartbeatTimeoutMs 10000 Liveness proof deadline after a ping. shutdownGraceMs 5000 Maximum Hub shutdown drain period. All durations, sizes, rates and counts must be positive safe integers, and the configuration validates the timing, capacity, duration, burst, buffering and heartbeat relationships. A relay session pauses at high-water, resumes below low-water, and only times out while high-water pressure persists.

A target becomes a Realtime target only when it is concrete, has canonical provider: openai, has a non-empty top-level apiKey, and declares realtime.enabled: true: aiTargets: - id: openai-realtime provider: openai apiKey: ${OPENAI_API_KEY} options: model: gpt-realtime-2.1 realtime: enabled: true maxSessionDurationMs: 300000 Eligibility: Legacy targets: entries cannot relay Realtime sessions. Composite targets cannot relay Realtime sessions. Non-OpenAI providers are not supported. Target realtime values may only tighten maxSessionDurationMs, idleTimeoutMs, maxMessageBytes and maxBytesPerSecond; they cannot broaden a global policy. The effective model is the optional client model query value first, then the target's options.model default. Admission fails when neither is available. Provider-side endpoints default to https://api.openai.com/v1, mapped to wss://.../realtime?model=.... Custom HTTPS endpoints are supported; plaintext http/ws is permitted only for loopback development and test endpoints. Endpoint user information, settings.apiKey, and configured overrides of the authorization, WebSocket handshake, OpenAI organization/project or safety headers are rejected. Provider compression is disabled. Rotating credentials Restart the Hub after changing a Realtime target's credential. Live credential rotation is not supported.

AI-Kit clients need no change: /realtime?model=<optional visible-ASCII model> Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: realtime, proactions-auth.Bearer.<token>, proactions-target.<target>, ... The query accepts only one optional model. The protocol must offer exactly one realtime, one bearer credential and one target; optional proactions-article.<label> and proactions-action.<label> entries are bounded correlation labels. The Hub selects only realtime. The Hub delays client-side acceptance until provider readiness — the first valid provider-side session.created event, which is delivered unchanged as the first client-side event. Admission has a 9 s deadline; AI-Kit expects the browser upgrade within 10 s and provider readiness within 15 s. After acceptance, text and binary frames remain transparent and ordered in both directions.

The ingress in front of the Hub must: forward the WebSocket Upgrade and Connection headers disable proxy buffering for these paths use long-lived upstream read/send timeouts exceeding the configured session duration strip external prefixes so the Hub receives /realtime or /proactions/realtime — for example rewrite /swing/proactions-dev/proactions/realtime to /proactions/realtime, or strip the ProActions prefix too for /realtime not terminate or rewrite the Realtime subprotocol header
Code Meaning 1009 Oversized message 1008 Policy, rate, or backpressure violation 1011 Transport failure 1012 Hub restart (server-side shutdown)

Disabled Realtime is readiness healthy and skipped. Enabled Realtime is ready only while its listener remains attached to the actual Hub server and the module is not draining. Readiness never probes OpenAI. On shutdown the Hub enters draining, rejects new admissions with 503, cancels pending admissions, closes active client sides with 1012 Service Restart, closes provider sides, waits at most shutdownGraceMs, then terminates leftovers and finalizes capacity and usage records exactly once.

The Admin Panel Realtime tab exposes aggregate pending admissions, active relay sessions, admitted/rejected/completed/failed totals, directional bytes, duration summaries, and categorized rejection/close totals. Realtime usage is accounted separately: token totals split by modality (input text/audio/image, cached, output text/audio), the provider-response status distribution, input-audio transcription usage (billed separately from response tokens), and per-target/per-model breakdowns of sessions, responses, tokens, bytes and duration. Token and response aggregates cover closed sessions only; open sessions appear in a live list with request ID, target, model, correlation labels, start time, age and directional bytes. Lifecycle logs contain the request ID, target, model, bounded article/action correlation labels, phase, duration, byte totals, token totals and the terminal category. Diagnostics and logs never expose principals, credentials, safety identifiers, the raw Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header, transcripts, instructions, tool arguments, audio, raw events, provider-side content, or peer-supplied reasons.
The path the Hub received is not /realtime or /proactions/realtime. Check the ingress rewrite: a deeper prefix such as /swing/proactions/realtime reaches the Hub unchanged and is not a route.

Either main authentication is disabled/mistyped (Realtime requires auth.type: token or edapi), the bearer credential is missing or malformed, or the proxy stripped the Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header so the proactions-auth.Bearer.<token> credential never arrives.
The browser's exact origin is not in allowedOrigins. Entries are exact matches, and CORS settings do not apply to the relay.

The Hub could not establish the provider side. Check that the target's apiKey is valid, that the target is a concrete provider: openai entry with realtime.enabled: true, and that the Hub can reach api.openai.com:443.

The Tools module provides utility functions for content processing and extraction. This guide covers configuration and usage of available tools.
Configure the article extractor tool: tools: - id: extract type: article_extractor No additional configuration or API keys are required for the article extractor.

Extract content from a URL: curl http://localhost:${PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT}/tools/extract?url=https://example.com/article Response: { "title": "Article Title", "description": "Article description", "author": "Author Name", "published": "2024-01-15T10:30:00.000Z", "content": "Full article text...", "links": ["https://..."], "image": "https://example.com/image.jpg" }
Each tool in the tools array has this structure: tools: - id: string # Required: Unique identifier type: string # Required: Tool type options: object # Optional: Tool-specific options
Field Description id Unique identifier for the tool (used for logging and references) type Tool type - currently only article_extractor is supported
Field Description Default options Tool-specific configuration options {}

The article extractor uses @extractus/article-extractor to extract content from web pages. Configuration​ tools: - id: extract type: article_extractor Endpoint​ GET /tools/extract?url={url} Parameters​ Parameter Type Required Description url string Yes URL of the web page to extract Response Fields​ The extractor returns the following fields (when available): Field Description title Article title description Meta description or summary author Author name(s) published Publication date (ISO 8601) content Main article text content links Array of URLs found in the article image Featured image URL url Source URL source Source domain Example Usage​ Basic extraction: curl http://localhost:${PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT}/tools/extract?url=https://blog.example.com/article-title Response: { "title": "How to Configure ProActions Hub", "description": "A comprehensive guide to configuring ProActions Hub", "author": "Jane Developer", "published": "2024-01-15T10:30:00.000Z", "content": "ProActions Hub is a powerful tool...", "links": [ "https://docs.example.com", "https://github.com/example/repo" ], "image": "https://blog.example.com/images/cover.jpg", "url": "https://blog.example.com/article-title", "source": "blog.example.com" } Supported Content Types​ The article extractor works best with: Blog posts and articles News articles Documentation pages Medium articles WordPress sites Generic HTML pages with article content Limitations​ The extractor may have difficulty with: JavaScript-heavy single-page applications (SPAs) Pages requiring authentication Paywalled content Dynamically loaded content PDFs and non-HTML documents

Tool operations are logged when tools logging is enabled: logging: types: tools: enabled: true console: true file: false level: info Log output includes: Tool type and ID Request URL Extraction success/failure Processing time Error details (if applicable) See Logging Configuration for details.

Invalid URL​ Error: { "statusCode": 400, "message": "Invalid URL parameter" } Solution: Ensure the URL is properly formatted and URL-encoded. Extraction Failed​ Error: { "statusCode": 500, "message": "Failed to extract content from URL" } Solutions: Verify the URL is accessible Check if the page requires authentication Try a different URL with clearer article structure Check network connectivity from the container Timeout​ Error: { "statusCode": 504, "message": "Request timeout" } Solution: The target website may be slow or unresponsive. Consider configuring HTTP client timeout in hub settings.
All errors follow the NestJS standard format: { "statusCode": 400, "message": "Error description", "error": "Bad Request" }
Configure timeout for tool HTTP requests in hub settings: hub: http_client: timeout: 120000 # 2 minutes for slow websites maxRedirects: 5
Tools use the same HTTP client configuration as the hub. To set a custom user agent, you would need to extend the tools module (contact your development team).

# Test with a known article URL curl http://localhost:${PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT}/tools/extract?url=https://example.com/article # Test with URL encoding curl "http://localhost:${PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT}/tools/extract?url=https%3A%2F%2Fexample.com%2Farticle"
If Swagger is enabled: Navigate to http://localhost:${PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT}/docs Find the /tools/extract endpoint Enter a URL Execute the request
Enable tools logging and check logs: # Podman podman logs -f proactionshub | grep tools # Docker docker compose logs -f | grep tools

URL encode parameters - Always URL-encode the URL parameter Handle extraction failures - Not all pages can be extracted successfully Cache results - Consider caching extraction results to reduce load Validate URLs - Validate URLs client-side before sending requests
Validate target URLs - Be cautious of SSRF attacks Rate limiting - Consider implementing rate limiting for extraction endpoints Content filtering - Be aware that extracted content is user-controlled

Set appropriate timeouts - Configure HTTP client timeout for slow websites Implement caching - Cache extraction results in your application Monitor extraction times - Track slow extractions through logging Use async processing - For large batches, process extractions asynchronously

Handle errors gracefully - Extraction can fail for many reasons Implement retries - Retry failed extractions with exponential backoff Log extraction failures - Monitor failure rates and patterns Provide fallbacks - Have alternative content sources when extraction fails

The tools module is designed to be extensible. Future tools might include: PDF text extraction Image processing Audio transcription Video processing Document conversion Custom Tools Contact your development team if you need custom tools added to the module.
Configure Logging to monitor tool operations Review Security Hardening for production deployments Operations Guide for monitoring and troubleshooting
The YouTube module provides OAuth 2.0 authentication and video upload capabilities for one or more YouTube accounts. This guide covers setup, configuration, and usage.

Before configuring YouTube integration, you need: Google Cloud Console project with YouTube Data API v3 enabled OAuth 2.0 credentials (Client ID and Client Secret) Redirect URI configured in Google Cloud Console Persistent storage for OAuth tokens

youtube: accounts: - id: main client_id: ${YOUTUBE_MAIN_CLIENT_ID} client_secret: ${YOUTUBE_MAIN_CLIENT_SECRET} redirect_uri: ${YOUTUBE_MAIN_REDIRECT_URI} token_storage_path: ./tokens token_storage_file: youtube_token_{id}.json Set environment variables: YOUTUBE_MAIN_CLIENT_ID=123456789.apps.googleusercontent.com YOUTUBE_MAIN_CLIENT_SECRET=your-client-secret YOUTUBE_MAIN_REDIRECT_URI=http://localhost:${PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT}/youtube/auth/google/callback?target=main Redirect URI The redirect URI must match exactly what is configured in Google Cloud Console, including the target query parameter.
Go to Google Cloud Console Create a new project or select an existing one Note the project ID
Navigate to APIs & Services > Library Search for "YouTube Data API v3" Click Enable
documents.s: Step 2: Enable YouTube Data API v3

documents.t: Navigate to APIs & Services > Credentials Click Create Credentials > OAuth client ID Select Web application Add authorized redirect URI: http://your-hub-domain:${PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT}/youtube/auth/google/callback?target=main Click Create Save the Client ID and Client Secret

Navigate to OAuth consent screen Select External (or Internal for workspace accounts) Fill in required fields: App name User support email Developer contact information Add scopes: https://www.googleapis.com/auth/youtube.upload https://www.googleapis.com/auth/youtube Add test users (if using External + Testing mode) Save configuration
youtube: accounts: array # Required: List of YouTube accounts token_storage_path: string # Optional: Directory for token files token_storage_file: string # Optional: Token filename pattern

Each account in the accounts array requires: Field Description Required id Unique identifier for the account Yes client_id OAuth 2.0 Client ID from Google Cloud Console Yes client_secret OAuth 2.0 Client Secret from Google Cloud Console Yes redirect_uri OAuth callback URL (must match Google Cloud Console) Yes
Field Description Default token_storage_path Directory path for storing token files ./tokens token_storage_file Filename pattern (use {id} placeholder) youtube_token_{id}.json

You can configure multiple YouTube accounts: youtube: accounts: - id: main client_id: ${YOUTUBE_MAIN_CLIENT_ID} client_secret: ${YOUTUBE_MAIN_CLIENT_SECRET} redirect_uri: ${YOUTUBE_MAIN_REDIRECT_URI} - id: secondary client_id: ${YOUTUBE_SECONDARY_CLIENT_ID} client_secret: ${YOUTUBE_SECONDARY_CLIENT_SECRET} redirect_uri: ${YOUTUBE_SECONDARY_REDIRECT_URI} token_storage_path: ./tokens token_storage_file: youtube_token_{id}.json Each account will have its own token file: ./tokens/youtube_token_main.json ./tokens/youtube_token_secondary.json

Initiate authentication for an account: curl http://localhost:${PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT}/youtube/auth/google \ -H "x-target: main" This returns a redirect URL: { "authUrl": "https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/v2/auth?..." }
Navigate to the authUrl in a browser Sign in to Google account Grant permissions to the application User will be redirected to the callback URL ProActions Hub receives and stores the tokens
Check authentication status: curl http://localhost:${PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT}/youtube/auth/status \ -H "x-target: main" Response: { "authenticated": true, "target": "main" }

Endpoint Method Description Public /youtube/auth/google GET Initiate OAuth flow No /youtube/auth/google/callback GET OAuth callback handler Yes /youtube/auth/status GET Check authentication status No /youtube/auth/logout POST Revoke tokens No Public Endpoints The callback endpoint (/youtube/auth/google/callback) is publicly accessible (does not require authentication) to receive OAuth redirects from Google.
Endpoint Method Description Public /youtube/upload POST Upload video with metadata No

Upload videos using multipart/form-data: curl -X POST http://localhost:${PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT}/youtube/upload \ -H "x-target: main" \ -F "video=@/path/to/video.mp4" \ -F "title=My Video Title" \ -F "description=Video description" \ -F "tags=tag1,tag2,tag3" \ -F "categoryId=22" \ -F "privacyStatus=unlisted" \ -F "thumbnail=@/path/to/thumbnail.jpg"
Field Description video Video file (binary) title Video title

Field Description Default description Video description Empty string tags Comma-separated tags None categoryId YouTube category ID 22 (People & Blogs) privacyStatus Privacy status: public, unlisted, or private unlisted thumbnail Custom thumbnail image (JPEG/PNG) Auto-generated

Common YouTube category IDs: ID Category 1 Film & Animation 2 Autos & Vehicles 10 Music 15 Pets & Animals 17 Sports 19 Travel & Events 20 Gaming 22 People & Blogs 23 Comedy 24 Entertainment 25 News & Politics 26 Howto & Style 27 Education 28 Science & Technology

OAuth tokens are stored in JSON files: ./tokens/youtube_token_main.json File structure: { "access_token": "ya29.a0...", "refresh_token": "1//0g...", "scope": "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/youtube.upload", "token_type": "Bearer", "expiry_date": 1234567890000 }
ProActions Hub automatically refreshes expired tokens using the refresh token. No manual intervention is required.

Revoke access and delete stored tokens: curl -X POST http://localhost:${PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT}/youtube/auth/logout \ -H "x-target: main" Response: { "success": true, "message": "Logged out successfully" }
Ensure the tokens directory is: Writable by the container user Not world-readable for security Backed up regularly (tokens are not easily recoverable)
podman run -v ./tokens:/usr/src/app/tokens:rw proactions-hub Persistence Tokens must be stored in a persistent volume. If the volume is lost, users will need to re-authenticate.

Request only necessary scopes: https://www.googleapis.com/auth/youtube.upload - Upload videos https://www.googleapis.com/auth/youtube - Full YouTube access Minimal scope recommendation: Use youtube.upload only if you don't need other YouTube API features.
Always validate redirect URIs: Use HTTPS in production Include the target query parameter in Google Cloud Console configuration Never use wildcards in redirect URIs
Protect token files: # Set appropriate permissions chmod 600 ./tokens/youtube_token_*.json # Ensure directory is not publicly accessible chmod 700 ./tokens
Never commit credentials to version control: # Good client_secret: ${YOUTUBE_CLIENT_SECRET} # Bad - never do this client_secret: your-actual-secret

YouTube operations are logged when YouTube logging is enabled: logging: types: youtube: enabled: true console: true file: false level: info Log output includes: Authentication events Upload operations Token refresh events Error details See Logging Configuration for details.

Initiate OAuth: curl http://localhost:${PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT}/youtube/auth/google -H "x-target: main" Visit the authUrl in browser Complete Google sign-in and grant permissions Check authentication status: curl http://localhost:${PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT}/youtube/auth/status -H "x-target: main"

curl -X POST http://localhost:${PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT}/youtube/upload \ -H "x-target: main" \ -F "video=@test-video.mp4" \ -F "title=Test Upload" \ -F "description=Testing ProActions Hub YouTube integration" \ -F "privacyStatus=unlisted"
Check that token file was created: ls -la ./tokens/youtube_token_main.json

Error: OAuth authentication failed Solutions: Verify client ID and secret are correct Check redirect URI matches Google Cloud Console exactly Ensure YouTube Data API v3 is enabled Check OAuth consent screen is properly configured
Error: redirect_uri_mismatch Solution: Copy the exact redirect URI from the error message Add it to authorized redirect URIs in Google Cloud Console Include the target query parameter
Error: No authentication found for target Solutions: Complete OAuth flow first Check token file exists in tokens directory Verify token storage path configuration Check file permissions
Error: Token has been expired or revoked Solutions: ProActions Hub should auto-refresh - check logs If auto-refresh fails, logout and re-authenticate Verify refresh token is present in token file
Error: Upload returns 4xx or 5xx status Solutions: Verify authentication is valid Check video file format is supported Ensure video file size is within limits Verify required fields are provided
Error: Insufficient permissions Solutions: Check OAuth scopes include necessary permissions Re-authenticate to grant additional scopes Verify account has permission to upload videos
Error: quotaExceeded Solution: YouTube API has daily quota limits. Check quota usage in Google Cloud Console and request increase if needed.
Use environment variables for all credentials Configure multiple accounts for redundancy Use descriptive account IDs for easy identification Test authentication after configuration changes
Use HTTPS for redirect URIs in production Protect token files with appropriate permissions Backup token files regularly Never commit tokens to version control Rotate credentials periodically
Monitor token expiration through logs Test refresh flow regularly Handle quota limits gracefully in client applications Implement upload retries for transient failures
Set appropriate video upload timeouts Compress thumbnails before upload Use background jobs for large uploads Monitor upload success rates
Configure Tools for content extraction Configure Logging to monitor YouTube operations Review Security Hardening for production deployments
This guide covers the initial configuration steps for ProActions Hub after deployment in a Docker or Podman environment.

Before configuring ProActions Hub, ensure you have: A running Docker or Podman container with ProActions Hub deployed Access to the installation directory (typically /methode/methdig/tools/proactions-hub/) Necessary API keys for the AI services you plan to use Network access to required external services (AI providers, EDAPI, etc.)

Your ProActions Hub installation should have the following structure: /methode/methdig/tools/proactions-hub/ ├── config.yaml # Main configuration file ├── tokens/ # YouTube OAuth tokens (optional) ├── .env # Environment variables (optional) ├── docker-compose.yml # Docker Compose config (Docker deployments) └── proactionshub.bash # Recreate Pod script (podman deployments) /methode/methdig/cluster/ └── start_stop_proactionshub.bash # Control script (Podman deployments)
The main configuration file is located at: config.yaml This YAML file uses environment variable substitution with the syntax: key: ${ENVIRONMENT_VARIABLE-default_value}

You can provide environment variables through: Container environment (recommended for production) .env file in the installation directory Direct substitution in config.yaml (not recommended for sensitive data)

Add at least one AI service target to enable AI-Link functionality: aiTargets: - id: openai provider: openai apiKey: ${OPENAI_API_KEY} options: model: gpt-6-luna max_completion_tokens: 12000 Set the environment variable: OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-your-api-key-here
documents.s: Step 2: Configure at Least One AI Target

documents.t: Configure EDAPI authentication: auth: enabled: true type: edapi edapi_url: ${EDAPI_URL} session: store: memory cookie: secret: ${PROACTIONS_SESSION_SECRET} Set environment variables: EDAPI_URL=https://your-edapi-instance/edapi PROACTIONS_SESSION_SECRET=your-random-secret-here Production Security Always use a strong, randomly-generated session secret in production. Never commit secrets to version control.

After making configuration changes: For Podman: cd /methode/methdig/tools/proactions-hub/ bash proactionshub.bash start_stop_proactionshub.bash start For Docker: cd /methode/methdig/tools/proactions-hub/ docker compose down docker compose up -d Check if the service is running: curl http://localhost:$PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT/health Expected response: {"status":"ok"}
ProActions Hub requires the following volumes to be mounted:
Mount your configuration file into the container: ./config.yaml:/usr/src/app/dist/config.yaml:ro Read-Only Mount The configuration file should be mounted read-only (:ro) for security.
If using YouTube integration, mount a persistent volume for tokens: ./tokens:/usr/src/app/tokens:rw This directory stores OAuth tokens and must be writable by the container.

ProActions Hub uses one port: Main API Port (default: $PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT) - HTTP/HTTPS API endpoints Only expose the main API port to your network: Podman: -p $PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT:3000 Docker Compose: ports: - "${PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT}:3000
If deploying behind a reverse proxy or load balancer, configure trust proxy settings: hub: security: trustProxy: true # or proxy server ip See the Security Hardening guide for details.
ProActions Hub provides health check endpoints for monitoring and load balancer integration.

Liveness: GET /health - Returns 200 if the application is running Readiness: GET /ready - Returns 200 when the memory and disk checks, MCP, the Realtime listener (when enabled), and — only when legacy targets exist — the legacy AI gateway are healthy
Configure your load balancer to use: Health check path: /health Healthy status code: 200 Check interval: 30 seconds (recommended)
ProActions Hub validates configuration on startup using Joi schemas.

By default, schema validation is enabled. You can skip validation for development: validation: skipSchemaValidation: false # Skip structure/type validation Environment variables: PROACTIONS_SKIP_SCHEMA_VALIDATION=false Production Warning Never skip validation in production environments. Validation catches configuration errors early.
Configure HTTP client timeout for AI requests: hub: http_client: timeout: 120000 # 2 minutes in milliseconds maxRedirects: 5
Configure TLS certificates: hub: tls: enabled: true cert: ${TLS_CERT_PATH} key: ${TLS_KEY_PATH} ca: ${TLS_CA_PATH} Mount certificate files into the container and set environment variables.
Enable Swagger UI for API testing: swagger: enabled: true path: docs Access at: http://localhost:${PROACTIONS_HUB_PORT}/docs Development Only Disable Swagger in production environments

Now that you have a basic configuration running: Configure AI-Link targets for your AI providers Set up logging for monitoring and compliance Apply security hardening for production Review operations guide for maintenance procedures
Once Hub is running with at least one AI target, you can use it from any ProActions workflow. Below is the complete path from Hub configuration to a working YAML action.

# config.yaml (on the Hub server) aiTargets: - id: openai # logical name you choose — used as "target" in YAML provider: openai apiKey: ${OPENAI_API_KEY} options: model: gpt-6-luna max_completion_tokens: 12000

Point the HUB service entry at the Hub endpoint and specify which target to use: # /SysConfig/pro-actions.ai-kit.yaml AI_KIT: SERVICES: HUB: endpoint: '{BASE_URL}/swing/proactions' # {BASE_URL} = current Swing instance target: openai # must match target.id in config.yaml defaultBehavior: | You are a professional writing assistant. Answer concisely and in the language of the article. SECTIONS: - !include /SysConfig/ProActions/sections/my-actions.ai-kit.section.yaml

Any HUB_COMPLETION, HUB_SPEECH, HUB_TRANSCRIPTION, or HUB_IMAGE_GENERATION step automatically routes through the HUB service you declared above: # /SysConfig/ProActions/sections/my-actions.ai-kit.section.yaml section: Content Generation context: story actions: - title: 'Summarize Article' flow: # Call the AI service through Hub — no API key in YAML - step: HUB_COMPLETION instruction: 'Write a two-sentence summary of this article: {textContent}' # Display the result and let the user accept or cancel - step: SHOW_RESPONSE message: '{{ flowContext.text }}' onError: - step: SHOW_NOTIFICATION notificationType: error message: 'Hub unavailable: {{ flowContext.error }}'
documents.s: 3. ProActions YAML — use the service in a flow

documents.t: HUB_VOICE_AGENT does not use the HTTP /v1 endpoints above. It opens a persistent WebSocket to the dedicated /proactions/realtime relay and therefore requires a separate service base URL and an OpenAI Realtime-capable target. # config.yaml on the Hub server aiTargets: - id: openai-realtime provider: openai apiKey: ${OPENAI_API_KEY} options: model: gpt-realtime-2.1 realtime: enabled: true The hub.realtime block (origin policy, safety secret, session and rate limits) must also be enabled, and main authentication must be auth.type: token or edapi. See Realtime Relay. # /SysConfig/ProActions/services.ai-kit.services.yaml HUB_REALTIME: # HUB_VOICE_AGENT appends /proactions/realtime. endpoint: '{BASE_URL}/swing' target: openai-realtime model: gpt-realtime-2.1 - step: HUB_VOICE_AGENT service: HUB_REALTIME behavior: | You are a helpful voice assistant. Call end_session only after the user confirms they are done. Before enabling this flow, verify that the deployed Hub version includes the Realtime relay. Requires ProActions Hub 1.3.0 or later. The Hub or its ingress must: Expose WSS /proactions/realtime Accept the EDAPI or Hub token and target metadata sent through Sec-WebSocket-Protocol Preserve WebSocket upgrade and subprotocol headers through every reverse proxy Use trusted TLS when the CMS is served over HTTPS Allow long-lived connections for at least the configured voice-session duration Permit outbound WSS access to api.openai.com:443 The client must run in Swing or Prime with an available EDAPI token. Browser CSP and firewalls must permit WSS access to Hub. A Hub deployment that exposes only the endpoints listed under AI-Link is not sufficient. AI-Kit verifies both connection phases automatically before microphone capture: the browser-to-Hub upgrade must select the realtime subprotocol, and Hub must return OpenAI's session.created event within 15 seconds. Failures identify whether to inspect the relay/proxy/authentication phase or the target/credential/egress phase. Verify the deployment by starting a Hub voice flow with browser developer tools open. The Network panel must show /proactions/realtime?model=... upgrading with status 101 and selecting the realtime subprotocol. Hub logs must show the request ID, selected target and model (user identities are never logged), and successful upstream OpenAI connection. Interpret 404 as a missing relay, 401/403 as authentication or subprotocol-forwarding failure, and an upstream connection error as target credentials or egress failure. See Voice Agents for browser requirements, complete flow examples, VAD controls, tools, outputs, and troubleshooting.

If you have multiple Hub targets configured (e.g., openai and claude), you can override the default at the step level without changing the service declaration: # config.yaml — two targets aiTargets: - id: openai provider: openai apiKey: ${OPENAI_API_KEY} options: model: gpt-6.1-sol - id: claude provider: anthropic apiKey: ${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY} options: model: claude-opus-5-5 # YAML — per-step target override - step: HUB_COMPLETION instruction: 'Draft a headline: {textContent}' target: claude # overrides the section-level HUB.target for this step only
documents.s: 4. Switching targets at the action level

documents.t: Both options above (target: within a single service, multiple service declarations) share the same HUB service definition. A third option is to declare multiple service definitions in SERVICES: and tell a specific step to use one of them via the service: property. This is useful when two service definitions need different defaultBehavior, endpoint, or other settings that cannot be changed per-step via target: alone: # /SysConfig/pro-actions.ai-kit.yaml AI_KIT: SERVICES: HUB: endpoint: '{BASE_URL}/swing/proactions' target: openai defaultBehavior: | You are a professional writing assistant. HUB_TRANSLATE: endpoint: '{BASE_URL}/swing/proactions' target: openai defaultBehavior: | You are a professional translator. Preserve formatting and tone. Return only the translated text, no explanations. # In a flow — pick the service definition per step - step: HUB_COMPLETION instruction: 'Improve this text: {selectedText}' # service: not set — uses the default HUB service - step: HUB_COMPLETION instruction: 'Translate to French: {selectedText}' service: HUB_TRANSLATE # uses the HUB_TRANSLATE service definition instead service: is supported on all service-aware steps, not just HUB_COMPLETION. For example, if you have two DeepL configurations pointing to different API plans, you can switch between them the same way: SERVICES: DEEPL: endpoint: /swing/proactions/proxy/forward/deepl DEEPL_PRO: endpoint: /swing/proactions/proxy/forward/deepl-pro # In flow: - step: DEEPL_TRANSLATE instruction: '{selectedText}' target_lang: FR service: DEEPL_PRO # use the PRO plan service definition for this step For the full list of HUB_COMPLETION options, see the HUB_COMPLETION step reference.
documents.s: 5. Using a different service definition at the step level

documents.t: Check logs for configuration errors: Podman: podman logs -f proactionshub Docker: docker compose logs -f
Look for validation error messages in logs: Configuration validation failed: "hub.port" must be a number Fix the configuration error and restart the service.

If /health returns non-200 status: /health is liveness only: a non-200 means the process itself is unhealthy — check the container logs for startup or configuration errors. For /ready, inspect the JSON body for the failing check. The legacy gateway check (ai_gateway) only applies while legacy targets exist; otherwise it reports skipped: true. Verify network connectivity to AI providers.
Ensure environment variables are: Set before container start Properly formatted in config.yaml: ${VAR-default} Not containing special characters that need escaping

ProActions Hub allows you to register and run custom MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers. This enables you to extend the Hub's capabilities with specialized tools, data sources, or workflows written in Node.js, Python, or other languages.

To run custom scripts, you must make them available to the ProActions Hub container. The recommended approach is to mount a host directory containing your scripts into the container at runtime. For example, to mount a local directory ./local/scripts to /usr/src/app/custom-scripts in the container: -v ./local/scripts:/usr/src/app/custom-scripts:ro
You can run Node.js-based MCP servers using the node executable or npx.

Here is an example of a simple weather-server.js using the @modelcontextprotocol/sdk. File: weather-server.js #!/usr/bin/env node import { Server } from '@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/index.js'; import { StdioServerTransport } from '@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/server/stdio.js'; import { CallToolRequestSchema, ListToolsRequestSchema } from '@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/types.js'; const server = new Server( { name: 'weather-server', version: '1.0.0', }, { capabilities: { tools: {}, }, }, ); server.setRequestHandler(ListToolsRequestSchema, async () => { return { tools: [ { name: 'get_weather', description: 'Get current weather for a location', inputSchema: { type: 'object', properties: { location: { type: 'string' }, }, required: ['location'], }, }, ], }; }); server.setRequestHandler(CallToolRequestSchema, async (request) => { if (request.params.name === 'get_weather') { const { location } = request.params.arguments; return { content: [{ type: 'text', text: `Sunny in ${location}` }], }; } throw new Error('Tool not found'); }); async function main() { const transport = new StdioServerTransport(); await server.connect(transport); } main().catch(console.error);

Add the server to your config.yaml. Using node for local scripts: mcp: servers: - name: weather command: node args: - /usr/src/app/custom-scripts/weather-server.js Using npx for published packages: mcp: servers: - name: sqlite command: npx args: - -y - '@modelcontextprotocol/server-sqlite' - '--file' - '/usr/src/app/custom-scripts/my-db.sqlite'
For Python servers, we recommend using uv to manage dependencies and execution. This allows you to define dependencies directly in the script.

Here is an example of an echo.py server using fastmcp. File: echo.py # /// script # dependencies = [ # "mcp[cli]" # ] # /// from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP mcp = FastMCP("Echo") @mcp.tool() def echo(message: str) -> str: """Echo back the message""" return f"Echo: {message}" if __name__ == "__main__": mcp.run()
Configure the server to use uv in config.yaml: mcp: servers: - name: echo command: uv args: - run - /usr/src/app/custom-scripts/echo.py

To deploy with custom servers, run the container with the volume mount: Docker: docker run -d \ -p 3000:3000 \ -v ./config/config.yaml:/usr/src/app/dist/config.yaml \ -v ./my-local-scripts:/usr/src/app/custom-scripts:ro \ artifactory.eidosmedia.sh/docker-releases/proactions/proactions-hub:latest Podman: podman run -d \ -p 3000:3000 \ -v ./config/config.yaml:/usr/src/app/dist/config.yaml \ -v ./my-local-scripts:/usr/src/app/custom-scripts:ro \ artifactory.eidosmedia.sh/docker-releases/proactions/proactions-hub:latest

The MCP Gateway allows ProActions Hub to host and connect to Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. This enables the ProActions Browser Client (Swing/Prime) to access backend tools, filesystems, databases, and other resources through a standardized protocol. Third-Party Software Disclaimer Enabling the MCP Gateway allows the dynamic installation and execution of third-party software packages (via npx, uv, pip, etc.) from external sources such as npm and PyPI. Important: These packages are not provided, maintained, or audited by Eidosmedia. Eidosmedia assumes no responsibility for the security, stability, or licensing of any third-party MCP servers or tools you choose to run. You are solely responsible for vetting and trusting the MCP servers you configure. Ensure your environment has appropriate network security controls (firewalls, egress filtering) to restrict what these tools can access.

Multi-Transport Support: Connects to MCP servers via stdio, http, or websocket transports. Remote Server Support: Connect to remote MCP servers over HTTP (Streamable HTTP) or WebSocket. Dynamic Execution: Spawns local MCP servers on demand using npx, python, uv, or other allowed commands. Security: Strict command allowlist and path traversal protection for local servers. Lifecycle Management: Auto-connect/disconnect, graceful shutdown, connection timeouts, and cleanup. Monitoring: Health and statistics tracking for all connected servers.
MCP servers are configured in the config.yaml file under the mcp section.

The MCP Gateway supports three transport types for connecting to MCP servers: Transport Description Use Case stdio Spawns a local subprocess and communicates via stdin/stdout (default) Local tools, npm/Python packages http Connects to a remote server via Streamable HTTP (POST for requests, SSE for responses) Remote MCP servers with HTTP endpoints websocket Connects to a remote server via WebSocket Real-time remote MCP servers

Use stdio transport (the default) to spawn local MCP servers as subprocesses. mcp: servers: - name: filesystem transport: stdio # Optional, stdio is the default command: npx args: ['-y', '@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem', '/tmp'] autoConnect: false env: NODE_ENV: production

Use http transport to connect to remote MCP servers via Streamable HTTP. This is ideal for centralized MCP servers or third-party hosted services. mcp: servers: - name: remote-tools transport: http url: https://mcp.example.com/v1 headers: Authorization: "Bearer ${REMOTE_MCP_TOKEN}" autoConnect: true connectTimeout: 15000 toolTimeout: 30000 Authentication Use the headers option to pass authentication tokens or API keys to remote HTTP servers. Environment variable substitution is supported.

Use websocket transport to connect to remote MCP servers via WebSocket for low-latency, bidirectional communication. mcp: servers: - name: ws-tools transport: websocket url: wss://mcp.example.com/ws autoConnect: true

The Hub container supports both Node.js and Python-based MCP servers. Node.js (via npx)​ Use npx to run Node.js-based servers without manual installation. mcp: servers: - name: filesystem command: npx args: ['-y', '@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem', '/allowed/path'] Python (via uv)​ The container includes uv, a fast Python package installer and resolver. You can use uvx to run Python tools ephemerally. mcp: servers: - name: python-tool command: uvx args: ['mcp-server-package', '--arg', 'value']

Common Options (all transports)​ Option Type Default Description name string Required Unique identifier for the server. Used in the x-target header. transport string stdio Transport type: stdio, http, or websocket. autoConnect boolean false If true, connects to the server immediately on startup. connectTimeout number 30000 Connection timeout in milliseconds. toolTimeout number 60000 Tool invocation timeout in milliseconds. allowedTools string[] [] If set, only these tools are exposed (allowlist). ignoredTools string[] [] If set, these tools are hidden (blocklist). stdio Transport Options​ Option Type Default Description command string Required Executable command. Must be in the allowlist. args string[] [] Arguments passed to the command. env object {} Environment variables for the subprocess. http Transport Options​ Option Type Default Description url string Required URL of the remote MCP server (e.g., https://...). headers object {} Custom HTTP headers (e.g., for authentication). websocket Transport Options​ Option Type Default Description url string Required URL of the remote MCP server (e.g., wss://...).
Interact with the MCP Gateway via REST API endpoints. All endpoints require authentication.

Execute a tool on a specific MCP server. Endpoint: POST /mcp/invoke Headers: x-target: Name of the MCP server (matches config.yaml). Authorization: Bearer token. Body: { "tool": "read_file", "arguments": { "path": "/tmp/demo.txt" } } Response: { "content": [ { "type": "text", "text": "File content here..." } ], "isError": false }
Get a list of available tools from all configured servers. Endpoint: GET /mcp/tools Query Parameters: server (optional): Filter by specific server name.
Retrieve connection status and health metrics for all servers. Endpoint: GET /mcp/stats

For stdio transport, only specific commands are allowed to be executed. The default allowlist includes: node npx python, python3 uv, uvx Attempts to use other commands will result in a configuration validation error. Remote Transports The command allowlist only applies to stdio transport. Remote transports (http, websocket) do not spawn processes and are not subject to command validation.

The Gateway runs as a non-root user (1001). npm/npx: A writable cache directory (.npm) is configured in the container to allow npx to fetch packages at runtime. Python/uv: A writable HOME directory is configured to allow pip and uv to install packages. Path Traversal: Arguments are validated to prevent directory traversal attacks (e.g., ../).

When connecting to remote MCP servers: Always use TLS: Use https:// or wss:// URLs to encrypt traffic. Authenticate: Pass authentication tokens via the headers option (HTTP) or query parameters in the URL. Network Controls: Restrict outbound connections from the Hub container to only trusted MCP server endpoints. Validate Trust: Only connect to MCP servers you trust, as they can execute arbitrary operations. mcp: servers: - name: secure-remote transport: http url: https://trusted-mcp.internal.example.com/v1 headers: Authorization: "Bearer ${SECURE_TOKEN}" X-API-Key: ${API_KEY}

Least Privilege: Only map necessary volumes to the container (stdio). Read-Only: Mount configuration files as read-only. Environment Variables: Use environment variables for sensitive credentials (API keys) instead of hardcoding them. Timeouts: Configure appropriate connectTimeout and toolTimeout values to prevent hanging connections. mcp: servers: - name: secure-server command: npx args: ['-y', 'my-server'] env: API_KEY: ${MY_SECRET_KEY} connectTimeout: 10000 toolTimeout: 30000
